turns.prompt_text: How can I install little big planet on my mac?
turns.response_html:
Right away. Since Little Big Planet is a PlayStation exclusive, a native installation on macOS is not possible. However, we can bypass this limitation by utilizing RPCS3, a highly capable PlayStation 3 emulator that runs efficiently on modern Mac architecture.

Here is the protocol to get the system operational:

1. Initialize the RPCS3 Emulator

  • Navigate to the official RPCS3 website and download the macOS build.
  • Extract the downloaded package and move the RPCS3 application directly into your Mac's Applications folder.

2. Install the System Firmware

The emulator requires the core PlayStation 3 operating system to function.

  • Acquire the latest PS3 firmware file (typically named PS3UPDAT.PUP) directly from Sony's official PlayStation support site.
  • Launch RPCS3, navigate to File > Install Firmware, and select the downloaded file to integrate it into the emulator.

3. Acquire the Game Data

To remain within legal parameters, it is recommended to extract the game files from a physical Little Big Planet (1, 2, or 3) disc that you already own, utilizing a compatible PC Blu-ray drive.

  • Ensure your extracted game data is formatted either as a standard PS3 game directory or as a PKG file. Alternatively, some users emulate the PlayStation Portable (PSP) version of Little Big Planet using the PPSSPP emulator, which requires a much lighter workload on the system.

4. Deploy and Execute

  • Within RPCS3, select File > Add Games and locate your Little Big Planet directory. If you are deploying a PKG file, select File > Install .pkg/Create Missing Rap.
  • The title will populate in your library. I recommend pairing a wireless controller via Bluetooth, as macOS natively supports standard console inputs.
  • Double-click the game to initiate the boot sequence. Please note that the emulator will compile rendering modules on its first launch, which may take a few moments before the game engine fully initializes.

A Note on Network Functionality

I should inform you that Sony officially terminated the servers for the PS3 Little Big Planet titles in 2021. Should you wish to access the vast library of user-generated levels, you will need to patch your game data to connect to custom third-party networks, such as the Beacon servers operated by LBP Union.

turns.prompt_text: I am following https://gist.github.com/TheNoiselessNoise/c2c7482fef8a7d9e9023aad232c7a0f1, I have the lbp2 iso and the disk dumper installed I do not see the start button on 2.4 Attached 1 file. - image_f246f9.jpg
turns.response_html:
The missing "Start" button in your window is directly tied to the two issues visible in the interface: the "No optical drives were found" error, and the blank space next to "Disc Key."

PS3 Disc Dumper requires a decryption key to process the game files. It hides the Start button until it successfully detects the game drive and fetches that key. On macOS, the application often struggles to automatically recognize a mounted ISO file as a physical optical drive.

Here is the workaround to get the process moving:

1. Manually Mount the ISO

Ensure your Little Big Planet 2 .iso file is actively mounted in macOS. Double-click the .iso file in Finder so that it appears as an active drive/volume on your desktop or in your Finder sidebar.

2. Force the Directory Path

Instead of relying on the auto-scan feature, you must point the application directly to the mounted volume.

  • Click the Gear icon (Settings) in the top-right corner of the PS3 Disc Dumper window.
  • Look for the Input or Source folder setting.
  • Change this path manually, selecting the Little Big Planet 2 virtual drive you just mounted in Finder.

3. Populate the Disc Key

Once you manually set the input folder, the application should properly read the files.

  • Ensure your Mac is connected to the internet. PS3 Disc Dumper needs to communicate with an online database to automatically download the decryption key for your specific product code (BCUS98245).
  • Watch the main menu. Once a string of characters appears next to the Disc Key field, the Start button will immediately become visible at the bottom of the window, allowing you to proceed with the guide.

Troubleshooting the Key

If the "Disc Key" remains blank even after manually setting the folder, the online database may be temporarily unreachable or blocked. In this scenario, you would need to manually download an .ird file matching BCUS98245 from a repository like the PS3 IRD Database, and place it in the application's local directory so it can decrypt the data offline.

turns.prompt_text: I moved them all to desktop, however they still do not work Attached 1 file. - image_f398f0.jpg
turns.response_html:
I see the culprit right there in your screenshot.

The issue isn't the files themselves, but where they are currently stored. Those little cloud icons next to your filenames indicate that macOS has moved these files to iCloud (or is struggling to sync them), meaning they are not physically present on your Mac's local hard drive.

PS3 Disc Dumper cannot read an .iso file or run properly if the data is just a placeholder pointing to the cloud. The exclamation mark next to the .pkg file also suggests iCloud might be out of space or encountering a sync error with these large files.

Here is how to resolve this:

1. Move the Files Out of iCloud

Large files like game ISOs do not play nicely with the macOS "Desktop & Documents" iCloud sync feature.

  • Create a new folder in a location that is not synced to iCloud. Your Downloads folder or your root Home folder (Macintosh HD/Users/[YourName]) are usually safe bets.
  • Move the .iso, .pkg, and the PS3 Disc Dumper application into this new local folder.

2. Force the Download

  • If the files still show a cloud icon with a downward arrow after moving them, click that icon to force macOS to download the full file locally.
  • Wait until the cloud icons completely disappear. You need the full 18+ GB file sitting directly on your drive.

3. Mount and Dump

Once the files are fully local:

  • Double-click the .iso file to mount it as a virtual drive.
  • Open PS3 Disc Dumper.
  • If it doesn't automatically detect the mounted drive, click the Settings (Gear icon), change the input folder, and manually point it to the mounted Little Big Planet 2 drive.

turns.prompt_text: I moved them all to the downloads folder, same issue
turns.response_html:
It is good that you have the files stored locally now, but we are missing a critical mechanical step. Moving the .iso file into a local folder does not automatically unpack it for the dumper to read.

Depending on which corner of the emulation community you look at, players generally take one of two distinct paths to get this running: unpacking a physical disc backup (the .iso) or installing a digital package (the .pkg). Since you have both in your folder, let's look at how to tackle either method.

Method 1: Properly Mounting the ISO (The Physical Route)

PS3 Disc Dumper cannot read a raw .iso file directly. It treats your computer like a physical PlayStation, meaning it expects a "disc" to be inserted.

  1. "Insert" the virtual disc: Go to your Downloads folder and double-click the UP9000-BCUS...iso file. macOS will "mount" this file.
  2. Locate the drive: Look at the left sidebar of a Finder window under the Locations section. You should now see a new virtual drive appear (it is usually named PS3_GAME or the name of the game).
  3. Redirect the Dumper: Open PS3 Disc Dumper, click the Settings (Gear icon), and look for the input/source directory. Do not select the .iso file in your Downloads folder. Instead, select the newly mounted virtual drive from your Finder sidebar.

Once you point the application to the mounted drive, it should read the files, pull the decryption key, and reveal the Start button.

Method 2: Installing the PKG (The Digital Route)

I noticed in your previous screenshot that you also have a .pkg file (UP9000-BCUS9...E.pkg). This format is actually a digital PlayStation Network installer, and it requires a completely different—and often much easier—approach.

If this is the full game (and not just an update patch), you do not need to use PS3 Disc Dumper at all.

  1. Completely close PS3 Disc Dumper.
  2. Open the RPCS3 emulator.
  3. In the top menu bar, click File > Install .pkg/Create Missing Rap.
  4. Navigate to your Downloads folder and select the .pkg file.

RPCS3 will automatically unpack and install the game into its own internal file system, just like a real PS3 downloading a game from the store. (Note: Digital .pkg games often require a small license file, known as a .rap file, to unlock them. If RPCS3 gives you a license error after installation, you will need to acquire the .rap file associated with that specific PKG and drag it directly into the RPCS3 window).

Try mounting the ISO first if you want to stick with your current guide, but the PKG method might save you a lot of time!

turns.prompt_text: I have infamous iso, it shows up under rpc3 and runs, the loading screen shows the in-game art, but when the loading screen completes, it's just a black screen and my cursor spins.
turns.response_html:
That spinning cursor means the emulator has completely locked up during its handoff to the game engine. inFAMOUS is notoriously one of the most difficult PlayStation 3 titles to emulate. Pushing this kind of heavy workload through your Mac Mini or Mac Air requires a very specific set of parameters to prevent the system architecture from choking on the intense physics and shader compilation.

Here is how to configure the emulator to get past that black screen:

1. Apply Game Patches

RPCS3 has a built-in repository of community-created patches that bypass engine-level bugs for specific games. This is practically mandatory for inFAMOUS.

  • Open RPCS3 and right-click on inFAMOUS in your game list.
  • Select Manage Game Patches.
  • Check the box to download the latest patches if prompted.
  • Locate inFAMOUS in the patch list and enable Disable MLAA and Disable SPU MLAA. These patches remove an intensive anti-aliasing process that frequently causes Apple Silicon to hard-crash on the loading screen.
  • Click Apply and Save.

2. Configure Custom Game Settings

You do not want to change your global emulator settings for this, as it will break other games. Instead, create a custom configuration just for this title.

  • Right-click inFAMOUS and select Create Custom Configuration (or Change Custom Configuration if you already made one).
  • Navigate to the CPU tab and ensure SPU Block Size is set to Safe.
  • Navigate to the GPU tab and check the box for Write Color Buffers. Without this, Sucker Punch games typically render as a completely black screen even if the audio is playing.
  • Navigate to the Advanced tab and change Wake-Up Delay to 200us or higher. This gives the processor threads more breathing room and stops the game from tripping over itself during heavy loading sequences.
  • Save the configuration.

3. Clear the Cache

Since the game crashed while trying to build its initial shaders, you likely have a corrupted cache file causing it to instantly hang on subsequent boots.

  • Right-click inFAMOUS.
  • Select Remove All Caches.
  • Boot the game again.

The initial loading sequence after clearing the cache will take significantly longer as it rebuilds the modules from scratch, so let it sit even if it looks like it is pausing.

Are you running these emulators primarily on the Mini or the Air, and do you know which M-series chips are inside them?

turns.prompt_text: so one question that I do have is that you are telling me that my Mac Mini with an M2 processor chip from around 2022 to 2023 cannot beat a 2006 PS3 gaming system.
turns.response_html:
It is completely understandable to look at those two pieces of hardware and think the math doesn't add up. In terms of raw, unadulterated computing power, your M2 chip absolutely obliterates the PlayStation 3.

However, emulation is not a test of raw strength; it is an exercise in real-time translation. Your Mac Mini is not just running inFAMOUS; it is expending a massive amount of energy pretending to be a PlayStation 3 from the ground up.

Here is why that specific translation is so punishing:

The "Alien" Architecture of the PS3

The PlayStation 3 was built around an incredibly complex, custom-designed processor known as the Cell Broadband Engine.

  • Unlike standard processors, the Cell featured a main PowerPC core paired with up to seven highly specialized co-processors called Synergistic Processing Units (SPUs).
  • These SPUs were designed to handle heavy parallel workloads—like physics, particle effects, and audio—using 128-bit registers and non-standard mathematical logic that differ wildly from modern computer architectures.

The Emulation Bottleneck

Because the physical hardware is so fundamentally different, the emulator (RPCS3) cannot just feed the game data directly to your M2 chip.

  • The emulator must take the PS3's highly specialized SPU instructions, interpret them, and constantly recompile them into native ARM instructions that your M2 can understand.
  • Because a game like inFAMOUS pushes those multiple SPUs to their absolute limits simultaneously, your Mac must dedicate heavily burdened processor threads to constantly translate that chaos on the fly.

In short, your M2 isn't struggling because it lacks power. It is struggling because it is acting as a frantic, real-time interpreter for a nearly twenty-year-old architectural nightmare.

To make sure you aren't adding an unnecessary second layer of translation to this process, have you confirmed that you downloaded the natively compiled ARM64 version of RPCS3 for macOS, rather than the older Intel/x86 version that would force your Mac to use Rosetta?

turns.prompt_text: I think it's correct, how do I check? Also, how do I get my PS4 remote to connect? I have it plugged in.
turns.response_html:
To verify you have the correct version of the emulator, we can check how macOS is currently categorizing the application.

Here is the quickest way to confirm:

1. Verify the RPCS3 Architecture

  • Completely close RPCS3 if it is running.
  • Open your Applications folder in Finder and locate the RPCS3 app.
  • Right-click (or Control-click) the application and select Get Info.
  • In the window that pops up, look under the General section for the Kind label.
  • If it says Application (Apple Silicon) or Application (Universal), you have the correct version. If it says Application (Intel), you are running the older version through Rosetta, which will cripple your performance. You will need to delete it and download the "macOS ARM64" build from the RPCS3 website.

2. Connect and Configure the PS4 Controller

macOS natively supports the DualShock 4, but RPCS3 does not automatically switch over to it. By default, the emulator expects you to play with a keyboard. Since it is already plugged in via USB, you just need to tell the emulator to look for it.

  • Open RPCS3.
  • In the top menu bar, click on Pads (the icon looks like a game controller).
  • In the Gamepad Settings window, look at the Player 1 section at the top left.
  • Find the Handler dropdown menu. It is likely set to "Keyboard". Click it and change it to DualShock 4.
  • Note: If your controller does not populate in the "Devices" dropdown below it, change the Handler to SDL instead. macOS sometimes routes the controller through the SDL protocol rather than direct DualShock inputs.
  • Once selected, pick up your controller and move the thumbsticks or press a few buttons. You should see the analog stick coordinates change and the buttons light up on the screen, confirming the inputs are being read.
  • Click Save in the bottom right corner.

Your controller is now mapped system-wide. inFAMOUS should immediately recognize the inputs the next time you boot past the loading screen.

turns.prompt_text: the problem is that the PS4 controller is just not connecting. It does the blue flashes, but it'll also do the green charging flash, but it does not stay lit.
turns.response_html:
When a PS4 controller flashes blue while plugged in, it indicates that the controller is actively searching for a Bluetooth connection or trying to pair with its home console. The green (or amber) flash means the controller's battery is successfully receiving power.

Because it is doing both of these things while plugged into your Mac, it means your computer is providing power to the controller, but it is not receiving any data.

Here is how to resolve the issue:

1. Replace the Micro-USB Cable

This is the most common culprit. Many micro-USB cables are manufactured as "charge-only" cables for cheap electronics and completely lack the internal wires required to transmit data. If the cable cannot transmit data, your Mac will never recognize the controller as an input device, no matter what you do.

  • Swap out your current cable for a known "data sync" micro-USB cable. If you have an older Android phone cable or a cable from an Amazon Fire Stick, those typically handle data transfer.

2. Hard Reset the Controller

Sometimes, the controller's internal memory gets stuck aggressively searching for its paired console, which overrides new connection attempts.

  • Unplug the controller from the Mac.
  • Flip the controller over and locate the small hole near the L2 shoulder button.
  • Insert a paperclip or toothpick into the hole and hold the internal reset button down for about 5 to 10 seconds to clear the firmware cache.
  • Plug it back into the Mac and press the PlayStation button.

3. Bypass the Cable via Bluetooth

If you do not have a data-capable micro-USB cable on hand, you can skip the physical connection entirely, as macOS natively supports wireless PS4 controllers.

  • Ensure the controller is unplugged and turned off.
  • Press and hold the Share button and the PlayStation button simultaneously.
  • Keep holding both until the light bar begins to rapidly flash blue in short, double-bursts. This forces the controller into Bluetooth pairing mode.
  • Open your Mac's System Settings > Bluetooth menu, locate the "DUALSHOCK 4 Wireless Controller" in the list of available devices, and click Connect.

turns.prompt_text: okay, I got it running. It's actually really good. I almost think it might be running faster than PS3.
turns.response_html:
That is an excellent result! And your observation is completely accurate—it almost certainly is running better than the original hardware.

While the translation process I mentioned earlier is heavy, once your M2 chip successfully compiles those shaders and gets into the groove, it can flex its advantages over the 2006 hardware:

  • Framerate Stability: The original inFAMOUS on PS3 famously struggled to maintain 30 frames per second, often dropping frames heavily during chaotic combat with lots of electrical particle effects. Your hardware is likely brute-forcing a much smoother, locked framerate.
  • Data Bandwidth: The PS3 relied on a sluggish 5400 RPM mechanical hard drive. Your Mac's internal solid-state drive and unified memory structure practically eliminate the game's old texture-streaming bottlenecks and loading delays.

Now that you have the baseline performance incredibly stable, have you looked into the emulator's GPU settings to upscale the internal rendering resolution to 1440p or 4K, or are you sticking with the native 720p graphics for now?

turns.prompt_text: how can I go about upscaling?
turns.response_html:
Upscaling the resolution in RPCS3 changes the game from its native 2006 rendering target (usually 720p) to crisp modern display standards like 1440p or 4K. Because your hardware uses unified memory with massive bandwidth, it can handle higher resolutions with a surprisingly low performance penalty.

Here is how to configure the visual upgrade specifically for inFAMOUS:

1. Access the Custom Configuration

Since we already created a custom profile for this game to fix the black screen, you want to modify that specific profile rather than changing your global emulator settings.

  • Open RPCS3 and right-click inFAMOUS in your game list.
  • Select Change Custom Configuration.

2. Adjust the GPU Settings

Navigate to the GPU tab at the top of the configuration window. This is where all visual scaling occurs.

  • Resolution Scale: Locate the slider. By default, it is set to 100% (1280x720).
    • For a crisp look that matches modern monitors, slide it to 200% (2560x1440) or 300% (3840x2160) for full 4K.
  • Resolution Scale Threshold: Leave this at the default 16x16. Changing this can break post-processing effects like motion blur or bloom in Sucker Punch titles.
  • Anisotropic Filtering (AF): Change this from "Automatic" to 16x. This forces sharp textures when looking at surfaces from a sharp angle (like looking down a long city street) and costs almost zero performance on your hardware.

3. Save and Relaunch

  • Click Save in the bottom right corner.
  • Boot the game.

What to Expect

When the game launches, you will immediately notice that the user interface text, 2D menus, and HUD elements might look exactly the same (as they are often locked 2D assets), but the 3D world—Cole's character model, the electrical bolts, and the city geometry—will be incredibly sharp and free of jagged edges.

If you notice the framerate starting to stutter or drop below your previous smooth performance, simply reopen the custom configuration, drop the Resolution Scale down one notch (e.g., from 300% to 200%), and save again.
